rows.textLatex: Describe the basic structure and working principle of a programmable logic device with the help of necessary circuit diagram.
rows.solution:
A programmable logic device (PLD) uses stored configuration bits to select internal connections. Its external inputs then pass through the programmed logic to produce the desired output.

**Basic circuit.** The notes illustrate a one-output, ROM-style realization with four inputs. Two 2-to-4 decoders select one row and one column of a $4\times4$ array.

```text
A1, A0 → DL (2-to-4) → row drivers → rows 0–3
                                          │
                                  4×4 switch array
                               each crosspoint D_ij
                               is a diode in series
                                 with a switch
                                          │
A3, A2 → DH (2-to-4) → selects column sense amplifier
                                          │
                              read-enabled output → Y
```

At crosspoint $D_{ij}$, $i$ is the row selected by $A_1A_0$ and $j$ is the column selected by $A_3A_2$. A programmed configuration bit closes or opens the switch. A closed switch at the selected row and column gives $Y=1$ when read is enabled. An open selected crosspoint gives $Y=0$.

**Example.** Closing $D_{00}, D_{03}, D_{12}, D_{13}, D_{21}, D_{33}$ gives $Y=1$ for input words `0000`, `1100`, `1001`, `1101`, `0110`, and `1111`, respectively. Thus, with input order $A_3A_2A_1A_0$,
$$Y=\sum m(0,6,9,12,13,15).$$

note_ref.section: Basic structure of a PLD, with a ROM-style row and column array
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 1, functional block. Fig. 2, decoder and diode-switch array. Fig. 3, programmed crosspoints. Fig. 4, corresponding input words.

rows.textLatex: Why are diodes or transistors not used for MOS devices? Describe any one switching technology adopted in FPGA to implement configurable hardware.
rows.solution:
**(a) Why the diode and bipolar methods are unsuitable.** The question refers to the programmable-link methods described in the notes. The diode method uses a large avalanche current to make a permanent short. The bipolar method uses a fusible link. The programming current and resistance levels of these methods are incompatible with MOS memory impedance levels. MOS transistor switches are used in MOS circuitry.

**(b) SRAM-controlled FPGA switch.** An SRAM cell stores one configuration bit. Its output controls a pass gate that connects two routing wires.

```text
row wire ─────────[ pass gate ]───────── column wire
                        ▲
                        │
                   SRAM cell
```

- A stored `1` turns on the pass gate and connects the wires.
- A stored `0` makes the gate high-resistance and isolates the wires.
- Rewriting the SRAM bit changes the connection. SRAM is volatile, so the configuration must be reloaded after power-up.

note_ref.section: Avalanche and bipolar programmable links, MOS compatibility, and SRAM-based FPGA switches
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 5–6, diode and bipolar methods. Fig. 13, SRAM cell controlling the pass gate.

rows.textLatex: With the help of a block diagram discuss the functions of different components of a PAL device.
rows.solution:
### PAL architecture

```text
Inputs → Input buffers → Programmable AND plane
         (I and NOT I)       │ product terms
                             ▼
                         Fixed OR plane → Output buffer → Outputs
                             │
                             └─ Optional register or feedback to AND plane
```

**Input buffers.** Each external input supplies both its true and complemented values to the AND plane.

**Programmable AND plane.** Select the input literals for each product term by retaining the required connections and opening the others. For example, a term that retains $A$ and $\overline B$ realizes $A\overline B$. With $M$ inputs and $n$ product terms, the array has $2Mn$ possible fusible connections.

**Fixed OR plane.** Each OR gate receives a predetermined subset of the product terms. Thus each output is a sum of its assigned terms. The groups of fixed connections are shown by solid dots in Fig. 35.

**Output and feedback.** A buffer drives the output pin. A registered PAL can feed an OR output through a flip-flop. Depending on the device, an output can return to the AND plane, with optional inversion, for use in another product term. Fig. 36 shows this feedback arrangement.

note_ref.section: Programmable Array Logic (PAL) as PLD
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 35 (AND and OR planes) and Fig. 36 (feedback and register). Diagram simplified from the notes.

rows.textLatex: State the reasons for different speed performance of ICs.
rows.solution:
### (a) IC speed performance

The notes explain speed differences using **pin-to-pin propagation delay**. For a given signal path, a useful estimate is

$$t_{\mathrm{pd}} \approx L t_{\mathrm{wire}} + N_g t_g + N_s t_s,$$

where $L$ is interconnect length, $t_{\mathrm{wire}}$ is delay per unit length, $N_g$ and $N_s$ count the gates and programmable switches on the path, and $t_g$ and $t_s$ are their representative delays. Chips and mappings can differ in all three contributions. The fitter's choice of wire segments affects the implemented delay. The notes illustrate this model with a Xilinx CPLD. This part applies that model to the question on IC performance.

note_ref.section: Pin-to-pin delay and routing. The solution applies the note model to IC speed.

rows.textLatex: Draw and describe the structure of a macrocell used in Altera MAX 7000.
rows.solution:
### (b) MAX 7000 macrocell

A MAX 7000 logic array block (LAB) contains 16 macrocells arranged as two groups of eight. The programmable interconnect array (PIA) connects LABs and can also connect to I/O blocks.

```text
 PIA and local LAB interconnect
               │
     Programmable AND plane ── five local product terms
               │
               ▼                 Terms from other LAB macrocells
      Product select matrix ◀─────────────────────┘
         │         │
         │         └── Set, clear and array-clock paths
         ▼
      OR → XOR → Programmable register ──┐
            └── Combinational path ──────┤
                                         ▼
                         Output select → To PIA
```

1. **AND plane and product select matrix.** The AND plane forms product terms. The matrix selects terms from the AND plane or local LAB interconnect. The OR gate can use the five local terms and up to 15 extra product terms from other macrocells in the same LAB.
2. **OR and XOR stages.** The OR stage sums the selected product terms. The XOR stage supplies the next logic result to the register or to the combinational output path.
3. **Register and controls.** The notes show a programmable flip-flop with D, JK, T, and SR configurations, or transparent operation. The figure shows a selection between global and array clock paths and the set and clear control paths.
4. **Output selection.** The selector returns the registered or combinational result to the PIA for routing to other logic.

note_ref.section: MAX 7000 logic array block and macrocell
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 42 on p. 29. The diagram retains its PIA, product select, OR/XOR, register and output-select blocks.

rows.textLatex: Explain the process used in CAD system for configuring SPLD.
rows.solution:
### CAD flow for an SPLD

```text
 Design entry → Merge and translate → Optimize equations
      ▲                                      │
      │                                      ▼
      └───────── Fix errors ─────────── Device fitter
                          ▲                  │
                          │                  ▼
                          └─────────── Simulate SPLD
                                             │
                                             ▼
                                     Configuration file
                                             │
                                             ▼
                                      Programming unit
```

1. **Design entry.** Enter the required logic as an HDL description, a schematic, or a combination of both.
2. **Merge and translate.** Combine the design inputs and convert them to a representation suitable for the next stage.
3. **Equation optimization.** Simplify the logic equations and reduce required gates, flip-flops and connections where possible.
4. **Device fitting.** Map the equations into the target device's available logic and route the connections. Check pin assignments and timing constraints. Fitting determines the configuration bits that specify the switch states and reports any constraints it cannot meet.
5. **Simulation.** Apply testbench inputs and check the resulting waveforms against the intended operation. Correct any errors before programming. The notes also permit an earlier functional simulation after design entry.
6. **Configuration and download.** Send the configuration file or fuse map to the programming unit to configure the device. For a device supporting in-system programming, the notes show downloading through its JTAG port.

note_ref.section: Computer-Aided Design (CAD) and the final programming step
note_ref.verified_diagram: Fig. 43 (SPLD design flow) and Fig. 44 (simulation with a testbench).

rows.textLatex: With a simple example describe the transistor pair logic used is FPGA.
rows.solution:
### FPGA transistor-pair logic

The notes use the **Crosspoint Solutions FPGA** as an example. Its transistor pairs have a primed device in the upper path and an unprimed device in the lower path. For a shared logic input, the upper device conducts when the input is 0 and the lower device conducts when the input is 1. Programmable connections join the required pairs. The notes turn both devices of pair 3 off to isolate neighboring sections.

### Example from the notes

The wired circuit in Figs. 54–56 implements $f=ab+\overline c$ for its labeled input $c$. The following switch diagram groups the parallel and series connections of those figures. Brackets identify the devices using the figure's numbering and give their closed-switch conditions.

```text
 +5 V ──┬──[1′: a=0]──┬── m ──[1: a=1]──[2: b=1]── GND
        └──[2′: b=0]──┘

 +5 V ──┬──[4′: m=0]──┬── f ──[4: m=1]──[5: c=1]── GND
        └──[5′: c=0]──┘

 Pair 3 and 3′ are biased off between the two sections.
```

1. **First stage.** If $a=b=1$, devices 1 and 2 provide a series path from $m$ to ground. If either input is 0, device 1′ or 2′ connects $m$ to $+5\,\mathrm V$. Therefore $m=\overline{ab}$.
2. **Second stage.** If $m=0$ or $c=0$, device 4′ or 5′ pulls $f$ high. If both are 1, devices 4 and 5 pull $f$ low. Thus $f=\overline{mc}=ab+\overline c$.

The introductory expression on p. 38 writes $ab+c$. To realize that expression with the wiring shown, feed $\overline c$ to the circuit's $c$ terminal. The inversion follows directly from the closed-switch conditions above.

note_ref.section: FPGA Structure: transistor-pair logic and the complemented input in the worked example
note_ref.verified_diagram: Figs. 50–56. The equivalent switch diagram follows the wiring and conditions in Figs. 54–56.

rows.textLatex: What is difference between 'bit' and 'std_logic'? How many different states are available as per IEEE standards in VHDL? Write down their names and symbols. Write their priority list.
rows.solution:
### 1. `BIT` and `std_logic`

`BIT` is a predefined VHDL type with two values, `'0'` and `'1'`, and no resolution function. `std_logic` is the resolved form of the nine-valued `std_ulogic` type. Import it with `use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;` after `library ieee;`. The resolution function combines multiple driver values on the same signal.

### 2. The nine states

| Symbol | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `'U'` | Uninitialized |
| `'X'` | Forcing (strong) unknown |
| `'0'` | Forcing 0 |
| `'1'` | Forcing 1 |
| `'Z'` | High impedance |
| `'W'` | Weak unknown |
| `'L'` | Weak 0 |
| `'H'` | Weak 1 |
| `'-'` | Don't care |

### 3. Resolution priority

For the usual driven values, the table gives **forcing > weak > high impedance**. `'U'` dominates every driver value. Forcing `'0'` and `'1'` have equal strength, and a conflict gives `'X'`. A driver of `'X'` gives `'X'` unless a driver is `'U'`. In the weak group, opposing `'L'` and `'H'` give `'W'`. `'Z'` leaves an ordinary driver unchanged, and all `'Z'` drivers give `'Z'`.

A single `'-'` driver remains `'-'`. With multiple drivers, `'-'` gives `'X'` unless a driver is `'U'`. For example, `'-'` with `'Z'` gives `'X'`. The table on p. 10 gives these pairwise results. Its explanatory priority list has inconsistent entries for `'-'` and `'Z'`.

note_ref.section: Signal types and logic states. The p. 10 table governs the examples.

rows.textLatex:
Compare (any Three):
(a) Harvard architecture and Von Neumann architecture.
(b) Microprocessor and microcontroller.
(c) Subroutine and ISR
(d) Timer and counter
(e) Internal RAM and Special Function Register
rows.solution:
### (i) Comparisons

Write any three in the exam. All five are covered here.

| Pair | First | Second |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Harvard vs. Von Neumann** | Harvard has separate instruction and data memories and separate paths. The CPU can fetch an instruction and access data at the same time. | Von Neumann (Princeton) uses a shared path for instructions and data. The two accesses compete for that path. |
| **Microprocessor vs. microcontroller** | A general-purpose microprocessor contains the CPU. The architecture in the notes connects memory and I/O externally over a system bus. | A microcontroller integrates the CPU, program and data memory, I/O, timers, and peripherals such as an ADC on one chip. It can also support external memory. |
| **Subroutine vs. ISR** | The running program explicitly calls a subroutine. On AVR it normally returns with `RET`. | An enabled interrupt transfers execution to its ISR after the current instruction. The AVR interrupt return instruction is `RETI`. |
| **Timer vs. counter** | In timer operation the register counts ticks from the internal clock, usually after prescaling. It measures time or produces a periodic event. | In counter operation the register counts selected transitions of an external input signal. It measures events. |
| **Internal RAM vs. special function registers** | Internal SRAM is general-purpose volatile storage for variables, buffers, and the stack. | Special function registers have fixed addresses and defined bit meanings. They configure or report hardware state, for example `DDRx`, `PORTx`, and `PINx` for port direction, output/pull-up control, and input reads. |

**Memory paths** (PDF pp. 34–35 of the overview).

```text
Von Neumann / Princeton
CPU ── shared address and data buses ──┬── Code memory
                                       └── Data memory

Harvard
Data memory ── data-side buses ── CPU ── code-side buses ── Code memory
```

note_ref.section: Microprocessor and microcontroller blocks, memory families, processor architectures, and AVR memory spaces

note_refs.section: Interrupt transfer to a service routine and return to the main program
Timer and counter operation, internal prescaler and external pulse input

rows.textLatex: What are the different types of memories available in a microcontroller?
rows.solution:
### (ii) Types of memory

- **Flash program memory** is nonvolatile and holds the program instructions. The program counter addresses the program space during instruction fetch.
- **SRAM data memory** is volatile and holds temporary variables, data buffers, and the stack.
- **EEPROM** is nonvolatile read/write data storage for values that must survive loss of power, such as settings.

The notes also classify memory more generally. The ROM family includes mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, and Flash. The read/write memory pages discuss SRAM, nonvolatile RAM, and DRAM. The three bullets above give the relevant ATmega2560 on-chip memory spaces.

note_ref.section: Memory families and AVR memory spaces

rows.textLatex: Mention the names of Special Function Registers in context with Timer operation. Draw schematically and write the bit formats of these registers for configuring a timer. State the functions of each of the bits.
rows.solution:
### (a) Timer registers and bit formats

Use Timer3 as the 16-bit example, as in the lecture’s CTC exercise. The timer clock comes from an internal prescaler or an external input. The counter `TCNT3` advances on each selected clock event. Comparing it with `OCR3A` sets `OCF3A` on a match.

```text
Bit       7       6       5       4       3       2       1       0
TCCR3A  COM3A1  COM3A0  COM3B1  COM3B0  COM3C1  COM3C0  WGM31   WGM30
TCCR3B  ICNC3   ICES3      —    WGM33   WGM32   CS32    CS31    CS30
TCCR3C  FOC3A   FOC3B   FOC3C      —       —       —       —       —
TIFR3      —       —    ICF3       —    OCF3C   OCF3B   OCF3A   TOV3
TIMSK3     —       —    ICIE3      —    OCIE3C  OCIE3B  OCIE3A  TOIE3
```

| Field or register | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| `COM3A/B/C[1:0]` | Select the action on each output-compare pin, such as disconnect, toggle, clear, or set. The available actions depend on the waveform mode. All three fields are `00` for software toggling of a normal GPIO pin. |
| `WGM33:0` | Select the waveform/counting mode and TOP. Use `0000` for Normal and `0100` for CTC with TOP = `OCR3A`. |
| `CS32:0` | Select the clock. Codes `000` through `111` select stop, internal clock divided by 1, 8, 64, 256, or 1024, then external falling edge and external rising edge, respectively. |
| `ICNC3`, `ICES3` | Enable the input-capture noise canceler and select the capture edge (0 falling, 1 rising). |
| `FOC3A/B/C` | Writing 1 forces the selected output-compare action in a non-PWM mode. |
| `TCNT3H:L`, `OCR3A/B/C H:L`, `ICR3H:L` | Hold the 16-bit current count, compare targets, and captured count, respectively. |
| `ICF3`, `OCF3A/B/C`, `TOV3` | Report input capture, compare matches, and overflow. To clear a flag by software, write 1 to that bit in `TIFR3`. |
| `ICIE3`, `OCIE3A/B/C`, `TOIE3` | Enable the corresponding interrupts. Interrupt service also requires the global interrupt enable. The program below polls the flag. |
| `—` | Reserved bit. Write 0. |

rows.textLatex: Mention the names of registers involved in configuring ADC of the microcontroller. How do you select a particular input channel and alter sampling frequency of ADC.
rows.solution:
### (a) ADC registers, channel selection and clock

| Register | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| `ADMUX` | `REFS1:0` selects the reference, `ADLAR` sets result alignment and `MUX4:0` supplies the low channel-select bits. |
| `ADCSRA` | `ADEN` enables the ADC, `ADSC` starts conversion, `ADATE` enables auto-triggering, `ADIF` flags completion, `ADIE` enables its interrupt and `ADPS2:0` selects the prescaler. |
| `ADCSRB` | `MUX5` extends channel selection. The trigger-source field selects the event used when auto-triggering is enabled. |
| `ADCL`, `ADCH` | Hold the conversion result. Read `ADCL` before `ADCH` when reading the full 10-bit result. |

For **single-ended** selection, use the following two banks. For example, ADC10 is PK2, so set `MUX5 = 1` and `MUX4:0 = 00010`.

| Selected channel | Pin bank | `MUX5` | `MUX4:0` |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| ADC0–ADC7 | PF0–PF7 | 0 | Channel index, `00000`–`00111` |
| ADC8–ADC15 | PK0–PK7 | 1 | Channel index minus 8, `00000`–`00111` |

```text
ADC0–ADC15 → MUX (MUX5:0) → 10-bit ADC → ADCH:ADCL
System clock → prescaler (ADPS2:0) → ADC clock ┘
```

| `ADPS2:0` | `000` or `001` | `010` | `011` | `100` | `101` | `110` | `111` |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Division factor $N$ | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 |

Changing $N$ changes the ADC clock $f_{\mathrm{ADC}}=f_{\mathrm{CPU}}/N$. At $16\,\mathrm{MHz}$ with $N=128$, the ADC clock is $125\,\mathrm{kHz}$. A normal single-ended conversion takes 13 ADC clocks, or $104\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ here. Starting each conversion in software adds loop overhead to the sample interval.

note_ref.section: ADC control and result registers, channel and prescaler selection, and the tutorial_19 polling example. The exam output uses an 8-bit port instead of the tutorial's serial monitor.

rows.textLatex:
Write short notes on any One:
(a) PORT programming
(b) RISC and CISC processor.
rows.solution:
### (a) ATmega2560 port programming

Each GPIO port has three registers. For bit `n`, `DDRx` controls the direction, `PORTx` holds the output or pull-up setting, and reading `PINx` samples the pin logic level.

```text
                         PORT x
                ┌──────────┼──────────┐
              DDRx       PORTx       PINx
            direction    latch      read pin
```

| `DDRx[n]` | `PORTx[n]` | Pin configuration |
| :---: | :---: | :--- |
| 0 | 0 | High-impedance input, internal pull-up off |
| 0 | 1 | Input with internal pull-up enabled, assuming global pull-ups are enabled |
| 1 | 0 | Output driving low |
| 1 | 1 | Output driving high |

In input mode, an external driver or pull resistor should define the level when the internal pull-up is off. In output mode, the latch drives the pin, while `PINx` reports the sampled pin level. Use masks to change individual bits without disturbing the rest of the port.

This example follows the notes' single-pin copy exercise. An external digital signal drives `PA5`. The level is copied to `PC7`, which may drive an active-high LED through a series resistor.

```cpp
#define inputMask (1<<PA5)
#define outputMask (1<<PC7)

void setup() {
    DDRA &= ~inputMask;
    PORTA &= ~inputMask;    // External digital input, no internal pull-up.
    PORTC &= ~outputMask;   // Set the initial output latch before enabling drive.
    DDRC |= outputMask;
}

void loop() {
    if (PINA & inputMask) PORTC |= outputMask;
    else                  PORTC &= ~outputMask;
}
```

### (b) RISC versus CISC

| Feature | RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) | CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Instruction design | Simpler operations with more regular encodings | Can express more complex operations in one instruction, often with variable-length encodings |
| Access to data memory | Typically uses explicit load and store instructions for data memory | Many instructions can use memory operands directly |
| Decode and execution | Regular encodings tend to simplify decode and pipelining | More complex decoding and a wider range of instruction latencies are common |
| Examples | AVR (including ATmega2560), ARM, PIC | x86, Motorola 68000 family |

These are architectural tendencies. Word length, cycle count, and speed depend on the instruction and implementation. RISC processors also use program and data memory.

note_ref.section: Port registers, individual-bit masks and the PA5-to-PC7 copy exercise.
note_ref.verified_diagram: Register block diagram on p. 20 and active-high LED circuit on pp. 60–61.

note_refs.section: RISC and CISC instruction-set characteristics and processor examples.
